title: Firm Foundations
subtitle: Five habits that decide whether a room stays tidy or goes back in a week.
objectives: Explain why an organised space reduces mental effort
State the five foundation habits of home organisation
Explain what giving something a home means
Explain the one in, one out rule and why storage is finite

cards.title: Tidying is easy. Staying tidy is the skill
cards.text: Anyone can clear a room in an afternoon. Whether it is still clear on Friday depends on habits, not effort.

cards.title: A tidy room is a room that asks less of you
cards.text: Every item out of place is a tiny unfinished decision. They are quiet on their own and loud in a pile.
points: **You scan a messy room** without meaning to.
**Every scan costs a little attention.**
**Finding things takes longer**, so you start later.
**This is not about looking neat.** It is about load.

cards.title: A pit crew works on a shadow board
cards.text: Every tool has its outline painted on the wall. A missing tool is visible instantly, from across the garage.
points: **One place per tool**, and it is drawn on.
**You do not search.** You look at the gap.
**Under two seconds** to find anything.
**That is a system**, not tidiness.

question.text: What is the main reason an organised room helps you?
options: It reduces the number of small decisions you have to make
It makes the room look expensive
It means you never have to clean again
It makes the room bigger
question.explain: Every item out of place is an unfinished decision. Fewer of them means less to carry around.

cards.title: Tap each habit
cards.text: Five habits, not five chores. Quiz questions come from all of them.

question.text: What does giving something a home mean?
options: It has one specific place it always lives
It is stored out of sight
It belongs to one person only
It is kept in your bedroom
question.explain: One place, always the same. If you have to think about where it goes, it will not go there.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: The five habits are set out. Part 2 is how to actually make them stick. Your place is saved.

cards.title: The habits are easy. Starting is the hard part
cards.text: Every one of these takes under a minute. What stops people is that a minute feels like it can always wait.

cards.title: Put it back, do not put it down
cards.text: Putting something down is not finishing. It is a decision you have handed to yourself later.
points: **Handle a thing once.** Finish the journey.
**Down means you decide again tomorrow.**
**Back means it is done.**
**Most mess is a pile of postponed journeys.**

cards.title: The two-minute rule
cards.text: If a job takes less than two minutes, do it now rather than remembering it.
points: **Remembering it costs more** than doing it.
**Hang the towel. Put the plate in.**
**Two minutes now** or twenty on Saturday.
**Set a timer once** and see how little it is.

cards.title: Pack the bag the night before, always
cards.text: Wraps, gloves, bottle, towel. Done at night it takes three minutes. Done in the morning it costs a session.
points: **Morning decisions are the worst decisions.**
**A packed bag by the door** removes them all.
**Same bag, same order, every time.**
**Nobody misses training** because of the bag then.

options: If a job takes under two minutes, do it now
Tidy for two minutes every day
Never spend more than two minutes tidying
Take a two-minute break between chores
question.explain: Remembering a two-minute job costs more than doing it. So do it and be finished with it.

cards.title: Your room is an inventory with no sort button
cards.text: In a game you sort chests by type without thinking about it. A real room needs the same decision, made once.
points: **Like with like.** Tools together, cables together.
**You search by purpose**, so store by purpose.
**Full chest? Something has to go.**
**One in, one out** is the same rule.

cards.title: One in, one out
cards.text: Space is finite and you already know it. This is the only habit that takes that seriously.
points: **New shirt in, old shirt out.**
**It keeps the total flat** instead of creeping.
**Without it, storage always loses.**
**Decide at the door**, not in six months.

question.text: Putting something down and putting it away are the same thing.
question.explain: False. Putting it down leaves the decision for later. Putting it back finishes it.

terms.def: Every object has one place it always lives.
Finish the journey now instead of leaving the decision for later.
If a job takes under two minutes, do it immediately.
Store things by what they are used for, not by size or colour.
When something new arrives, something leaves. Keeps the total flat.
A board with each tool's outline drawn on it, so a gap is visible at once.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **One home per object**, decided once.
**Put it back, never down.**
**Under two minutes? Do it now.**
**One in, one out.** Storage is finite.

quiz.text: Why does an organised room reduce mental effort?
options: Every item out of place is a small unfinished decision
Clean rooms are quieter
Tidy rooms have more space in them
It means you never need to clean again
quiz.explain: They are quiet individually and loud in a pile. Fewer of them means less to carry.
quiz.objective: Explain why an organised space reduces mental effort

quiz.text: What does it mean to give an object a home?
options: It has one place it always lives and returns to
It is hidden away in a cupboard
It is labelled with your name
It stays in the room you use it in
quiz.explain: One place, always the same. If you have to think about it, it will not happen.
quiz.objective: Explain what giving something a home means

options: A board with each tool's outline drawn on it
A dark board used for writing
A cover that keeps dust off tools
A list of jobs still to be done
quiz.explain: You do not search for the tool. You look at the gap where it should be.
quiz.objective: Explain what giving something a home means

quiz.text: Putting something down counts as putting it away.
quiz.explain: False. Down postpones the decision. Back finishes it. That difference is most of the mess.
quiz.objective: State the five foundation habits of home organisation

options: If a job takes under two minutes, do it now
Spend two minutes tidying each morning
Rest for two minutes between jobs
Never let a job run over two minutes
quiz.explain: Remembering a two-minute job costs more attention than just doing it.

quiz.text: Which of these should you do under the two-minute rule?
options: Hang up the towel as you leave the bathroom
Reorganise the whole wardrobe
Repaint the bedroom wall
Sort every photo on your phone
quiz.explain: It is for the small jobs. The big ones get a scheduled block instead.

quiz.text: What does like with like mean?
options: Store things by what they are used for
Store things by their colour
Store things by their size
Store the things you like most together
quiz.explain: You search by purpose, so store by purpose. Cables with cables, tools with tools.
quiz.objective: State the five foundation habits of home organisation

quiz.text: What is the one in, one out rule?
options: When something new arrives, something else leaves
Only one person tidies at a time
Only take one item out of a drawer at a time
Buy one new thing each month
quiz.explain: It keeps the total flat instead of creeping upward. Storage is finite and this respects that.
quiz.objective: Explain the one in, one out rule and why storage is finite

quiz.text: Storage space is effectively unlimited if you organise well enough.
quiz.explain: False. It is finite. One in, one out is the only habit that takes that seriously.
quiz.objective: Explain the one in, one out rule and why storage is finite

quiz.text: You pick up a jacket off the floor. Put these in the right order.
quiz.explain: Decide, travel, finish. Skipping the third step is exactly how a chair becomes a clothes pile.
quiz.objective: State the five foundation habits of home organisation

quiz.text: Why pack a training bag the night before?
options: It removes decisions from the worst time to make them
It makes the bag lighter
It is required by most gyms
It stops the kit smelling
quiz.explain: Three minutes at night, or a missed session in the morning. Same bag, same order, every time.

quiz.text: Which is a habit rather than a chore?
options: Always putting your keys in the same bowl
Cleaning the whole room on Saturday
Vacuuming the floor
Washing the windows
quiz.explain: A habit is small, repeated and automatic. Chores are what you get when the habits are missing.
quiz.objective: State the five foundation habits of home organisation

teacher.summary: Week 1 TLE covers the foundations of home organisation, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. The framing is deliberate and it matters more than the content: an organised room is presented as a way of reducing the number of small decisions a person has to carry, not as a way of looking neat. That is the version of this topic that is useful to a learner who finds sustained attention expensive, and it is also the honest one. The shadow board is the anchor image because it makes the abstract idea of 'a home for everything' physical and checkable. Every habit here is under two minutes to perform; the lesson is explicit that starting, not effort, is the obstacle.
discussion: Ask him to name three things in his room that have no home. Naming them is most of the work.
Try the two-minute rule for one evening and count how many jobs it catches. The number is usually surprising.
Ask what a shadow board version of his desk would look like. It turns tidying into design.
Ask what would have to leave for something new to come in. One in, one out only bites when it is specific.
teacher.extension: Have him choose one surface — a desk, a shelf, one drawer — and give every object on it a home, written down. One surface done properly beats a whole room done once.
misconceptions: 'Tidying and staying tidy are the same skill.' Tidying is a one-off effort. Staying tidy is a set of habits.
'Putting something down is putting it away.' Down leaves the decision for later. Back finishes it.
'Organising is about appearance.' It is about reducing the number of decisions a room asks of you.
'If I organise well enough I will not have to get rid of anything.' Storage is finite. One in, one out is the rule that admits it.
